questions.explanation: v1 (older code) must read records written by v2 (newer code), which is exactly forward compatibility. Backward compatibility is the reverse direction. Rolling upgrades are precisely when versions coexist, so compatibility can't be avoided.
options: Backward compatibility — newer code can read data written by older code
Forward compatibility — older code can read data written by newer code
Both directions at once, because every upgrade needs both
Neither — rolling upgrades avoid compatibility concerns entirely
questions.question: Your team does a rolling upgrade: new servers run v2 while some still run v1, and v2 writes records that v1 must still read. Which compatibility does this scenario require?

questions.explanation: Language-specific formats can typically only be read by the same language (often the same version), which breaks cross-language interop and future upgrades; they also have well-known deserialization vulnerabilities. Nesting works fine, size isn't the core objection, and they don't use schema registries.
options: It produces output that is too large to store efficiently
It ties the data to one language and runtime version, and deserializing untrusted data is a security risk
It cannot represent nested data structures
It requires a schema registry to decode the bytes
questions.question: Why does the book advise against using language-specific serialization (like Java's built-in serialization or Python's pickle) for data you store long-term or send to other services?

questions.explanation: Fields are matched by tag number, not by name, so reusing or repurposing a tag makes old and new code interpret the same bytes differently. A fresh tag lets old code simply skip what it doesn't recognize.
options: Reuse the tag number of a deleted field so numbering stays compact
Add the field with a brand-new tag number and never change what an existing tag means
Rename an existing field but keep its tag number
Add the field with a new tag but delete the oldest field to keep the schema small
questions.question: In Protocol Buffers or Thrift, you need to add a field to a record that old binaries will still receive. What is the safe way to do it?

questions.explanation: Avro ships the writer's schema (or a reference to it) alongside the data, and the reader reconciles it with its own schema using resolution rules — so the payload itself needs no tags, and readers aren't locked to the writer's exact version.
options: It requires the reader to always use the exact schema version the writer used
The reader resolves the writer's schema against its own schema at read time, mapping fields by name and type
It stores a full copy of the schema inside every single record
It forbids schema changes after data has been written
questions.question: How does Avro support schema evolution without embedding field tags or names in the encoded data?

questions.explanation: Dropping the explicit schema doesn't remove it: every reader and writer still assumes a shape, but now those assumptions live scattered in code with no tooling to catch breaking changes. JSON parses fine without schemas and tolerates new fields gracefully.
options: JSON cannot be parsed without a schema, so the data becomes unreadable
The schema still exists — it's just implicit in the application code, where nothing validates compatibility
Schemaless data cannot be compressed or indexed
JSON objects cannot gain new fields without breaking old readers
questions.question: A team stores everything as schemaless JSON and changes the shape freely. According to the chapter, what is the hidden cost?

questions.explanation: A database decouples writers and readers in time: the value you write now may be read months later by newer code, so new code must read old data. Databases don't rewrite everything on upgrade, and versions routinely differ across time.
options: Forward compatibility, because the database validates all writes
Backward compatibility, because data written today will be read by future versions of the code
Neither — databases rewrite all old data on every upgrade
Both equally, because readers and writers always run the same version
questions.question: In dataflow through a database, which compatibility direction matters most, and why?

questions.explanation: The network is not transparent: pretending a remote call is local hides failure modes that don't exist locally (e.g., a timeout where the call may still have executed). RPC can be fast, is often cross-language, and can use JSON.
options: They are always slower than REST for the same payload
They cannot cross language boundaries
They hide the reality of the network — timeouts, partial failure, and unpredictable latency — behind a local-call illusion
They require binary encodings and cannot use JSON
questions.question: What is the book's core criticism of RPC frameworks that try to make a remote call look like a local function call?

questions.explanation: The first two are the chapter's direct comparison. Binary encodings like Thrift, Protocol Buffers, and Avro absolutely use schemas, and JSON has no built-in schema language.
options: JSON and XML are human-readable and widely supported, but verbose compared to binary formats
Binary variants like BSON and MessagePack keep a JSON-like data model while being more compact
All binary encodings are schemaless by definition
JSON includes a built-in schema language, which is why it needs no external schema
questions.question: Which statements about text and binary encodings are true? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Adding optional fields plus ignoring unknown fields is the compatible path in both directions. Deleting or repurposing fields/tags breaks readers that still expect the old meaning.
options: Only add new optional fields; never remove or repurpose existing fields
Old code should skip or ignore fields it does not recognize
Immediately delete fields you no longer use to keep payloads small
Reuse tag numbers of removed fields to keep numbering dense
questions.question: Which practices keep schema evolution safe as producers and consumers upgrade independently? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Brokers actually decouple deployments — producers and consumers upgrade independently, which is precisely why messages must stay version-tolerant: consumers may lag several versions behind.
options: A database decouples producers and consumers in time — writes now, reads later, possibly by different code versions
REST APIs are organized around resources identified by URLs, with JSON as the common encoding
Message brokers force producers and consumers to deploy new versions at the same time
Using a message broker removes the need for version-tolerant message formats
questions.question: Which statements about the modes of dataflow are true? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Schemas give you documentation and a checkable contract, but they don't auto-guarantee compatibility — you still must follow evolution rules — and payload size depends on the encoding, not on merely having a schema.
options: They document the data and act as a contract all parties can check against
Compatibility tooling can reject breaking schema changes before they are deployed
They automatically guarantee forward compatibility with no further effort
They make every payload smaller than any schemaless encoding
questions.question: What do explicit schemas buy you, according to the chapter? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Protobuf/Thrift use numeric tags (not names) in the payload with schemas on both ends; Avro carries no tags and reconciles schemas at read time, which suits big files where the schema is stored once per file.
options: Avro resolves the writer's schema against the reader's schema at read time instead of using field tags
Protocol Buffers embed field names (not tag numbers) in the encoded bytes
Avro's design makes it a natural fit for large archival files, e.g. in Hadoop
Thrift and Protocol Buffers require both sides to have the schema; the data carries tags, not names
questions.question: Which statements correctly contrast Avro with Thrift/Protocol Buffers? (Select all that apply)

summary.overview: Chapter 4 is about how programs turn in-memory data structures into bytes for storage and transmission, and how those encodings must keep working as applications evolve. Because rolling upgrades and slow-updating clients mean old and new code routinely coexist, every encoding choice is really a compatibility choice. The chapter compares text vs. binary formats and schemaless vs. schema-based designs, then shows how evolution plays out across databases, service APIs, and message passing.

sections.heading: Formats for Encoding Data
takeaways: Language-specific serialization (Java serialization, Python pickle) couples data to one language and runtime version — don't use it for long-lived storage or cross-service communication.
JSON and XML are human-readable and universal but verbose; binary JSON-like variants such as BSON and MessagePack keep the same data model in a smaller payload.
Thrift and Protocol Buffers identify fields by numeric tags and require a schema on both ends; evolve safely by adding new tags and never reusing or redefining an existing tag.
Avro needs no field tags in the data: the reader reconciles the writer's schema with its own at read time, which makes it a good fit for large files such as Hadoop datasets.

sections.heading: The Merits of Schemas
takeaways: An explicit schema documents the data and serves as a compatibility contract, so tooling can reject breaking changes before deployment.
Schemaless formats don't eliminate schemas — they push them into application code as implicit assumptions, with nothing validating that producers and consumers still agree.

sections.heading: Modes of Dataflow
takeaways: Dataflow through databases decouples writers and readers in time, so backward compatibility matters most: data written today must be readable by future code.

REST is organized around resources and URLs; RPC pretends remote calls are local, hiding timeouts and partial failure — and both need version-tolerant APIs because clients upgrade on their own schedule.
Message-passing through brokers decouples producers from consumers, so messages must be self-describing and version-tolerant — consumers can lag producers by several versions.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Backward compatibility: new code reads old data. Forward compatibility: old code reads new data. You need both whenever versions coexist — rolling upgrades, mobile clients, independent services.
The safe evolution playbook: only add optional fields, never remove or repurpose fields or tags, and make old code ignore what it doesn't recognize.
